doc.title: Fred Wesley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 21, 2024

title: Skipping class for the band room; improvising blues before learning trombone
summary: Wesley says he learned to improvise blues before reading music, and preferred playing like Things Ain't What They Used to Be to classical piano.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Okay. All right. So I prepared some — My name is Monk Rowe for the Fillius Jazz Archive and I’m very pleased to have Mr. Fred Wesley with me today, a trombonist, arranger, composer, band leader, and as a high school student skipped his father’s social studies class to hang out in the band room.
I couldn’t leave. I tried to make my father’s social studies class. I couldn’t leave. I was in the middle of blues changes and I just couldn’t leave, I couldn’t leave for nothing.

One of my favorite subjects — was there a point where you were learning not only the trombone and the baritone, but you started to get this thing like okay there’s this blues form, what is this. Did someone show you or did it sort of just enter your consciousness because of the playing?

You know I learned how to improvise blues before I learned how to play the trombone you know. I was just playing stuff that was in my head you know. And then I found out when I got in my father’s band I had to read music and I had to learn how to play the trombone you know. So I learned what I had to learn after I learned how to improvise.

Did spending time at the piano help with the improvising? Because I know, I read in your book that you had the typical sort of classical lessons, but, I actually have a quote here. You wrote: “ I just didn’t want to be this Glen Howard guy who played the hell out of Rachmaninoff. I wanted to play the shit out of the trombone solo in “Things Ain’t What They Used to Be.”

Yeah, yeah. Well you know Gwen Howard was a girl. And I didn’t want to play that nice little dainty music like girls played you know. I wanted to play like “Things Ain’t What It Used to Be.” So that was in my head you know. I can play the boogie woogie on the piano with my left hand and in my right hand I played the chord. I didn’t know what I was doing but I was hearing it in my head you know. So that’s what I learned before I learned music. You know? I knew how to play, how to improvise and how to make up music before I knew how to write it down and what it was about to write it down. You know. In fact I didn’t learn that stuff until I got with James Brown, you know?
